stem: A histogram has unequal class widths. The class [20-30] has frequency 24 and width 10, while the class [30-50] has frequency 36 and width 20. If frequency density is plotted on the y-axis, which class has the taller bar?

options.text: Class [20-30], because its frequency density is higher
Class [30-50], because its frequency is higher
Both bars are the same height
Class [30-50], because its frequency density is higher

per_option_rationale.rationale: Frequency density of [20-30] = 24/10 = 2.4; frequency density of [30-50] = 36/20 = 1.8. Class [20-30] has the taller bar.
Using raw frequency (36 > 24) ignores unequal widths; for unequal-width histograms the bar height must be frequency density, not frequency.
The densities are 2.4 and 1.8, which are not equal.
Class [30-50] has lower frequency density (1.8 < 2.4); confusing the direction of comparison after correctly identifying the measure.

explanation: For unequal-width histograms, bar height = frequency density = frequency / class width. [20-30]: 24/10 = 2.4. [30-50]: 36/20 = 1.8. Class [20-30] has the taller bar despite having a lower raw frequency.

explanation_sections.punchline: Frequency density = frequency / width; [20-30] gives 2.4 vs [30-50]'s 1.8, so [20-30] is taller.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify the model: unequal-width histogram - bar height = frequency density = f/w. Compute both densities and compare.
explanation_sections.lesson: Raw frequency misleads when widths differ; always divide by width to get comparable bar heights.
explanation_sections.timing: 90 s. Quick division: 24/10 = 2.4 vs 36/20 = 1.8; no further steps needed.
